label: Orientations
notes: This chapter, printed pages 377 through 399, turns the vague idea of handedness into checkable sign data. We follow one thread from determinant signs of bases through orientation forms and oriented atlases to boundaries, non-orientable examples, and the orientation double cover.

label: Orienting a Vector Space
notes: Begin with linear algebra. Two ordered bases agree in orientation exactly when the change-of-basis matrix has positive determinant. This is an equivalence relation with precisely two classes, so a finite-dimensional real vector space carries exactly two orientations, one chosen as standard.

label: The Two Classes
notes: Make the two classes concrete in the plane. The standard frame and any positive shear of it both turn counterclockwise and sit in the positive class; a reflection flips the second arrow and lands in the negative class. The determinant sign is the entire content of the distinction.

label: Pointwise to Global
notes: A pointwise orientation assigns an orientation to each tangent space. Such a choice is an orientation of the manifold only when it varies continuously, meaning every point has a chart whose coordinate frame is positively oriented throughout. Manifolds admitting such a choice are called orientable.

label: Orientation Forms
notes: On an n-manifold a nowhere-vanishing n-form is an orientation form. It selects, at each point, the bases on which it evaluates positively, giving a consistent pointwise orientation automatically. Two such forms induce the same orientation when they differ by a positive function, so orientability equals existence of such a form.

label: Oriented Atlases
notes: The chart-based criterion: an oriented atlas is one whose transition maps all have positive Jacobian determinant on overlaps. The sign tracker contrasts identity and positive-shear overlaps, which preserve orientation, with reflection and coordinate swap, which reverse it and cannot belong to a consistently oriented atlas.

label: The Mobius Band
notes: The Mobius band is the standard non-orientable surface. Transport a transverse frame once around the central loop and it returns reflected, so no continuous global choice of orientation exists. The cylinder, by contrast, returns the frame unchanged, and so it is orientable.

label: Klein Bottle and RP^n
notes: Other non-orientable spaces share this monodromy. The Klein bottle embeds a Mobius band and inherits the flip. For real projective space the antipodal map on the sphere preserves orientation exactly when the dimension is odd, so RP^n is orientable precisely when n is odd.

label: Boundary Orientation
notes: An oriented manifold-with-boundary induces a Stokes orientation on its boundary by the outward-normal-first rule: a boundary frame is positive when prefixing the outward normal yields a positive ambient frame. This is the convention that makes Stokes' theorem hold without stray signs.

label: Boundary on the Disk
notes: On the oriented disk the rule forces the counterclockwise tangent. At each boundary point the outward normal then the induced tangent form a positively oriented pair, so the determinant of that ordered pair is positive everywhere. The picture and the sign computation agree exactly.

label: Riemannian Volume Form
notes: Add a Riemannian metric to an oriented manifold and you get a canonical volume form. In oriented coordinates its coefficient is the square root of the determinant of the metric, always positive. Reversing the orientation reverses the form while the underlying density stays positive.

label: Orientation Double Cover
notes: Every manifold carries an orientation double cover whose points are pointwise orientations. It is connected exactly when the base is non-orientable, and the base is orientable exactly when the cover splits into two sheets. Deck transformations that preserve orientation are the obstruction being measured.

label: Synthesis
notes: We close by stitching the thread together: determinant signs classify bases, orientation forms and positive atlases encode a global choice, boundaries inherit orientation by the normal rule, and the double cover detects when no global choice exists. Each claim points to a concrete sign, not a picture.
